channel.title: ada-media
channel.description: Daily build notes from an open-source project in progress.

item.title: Day 8 — the case of the phantom panels
item.description: An empty note and a media window appeared without being asked, and neither could be dismissed. Today's fix: panels that only exist when requested.
item.content:encoded:
What I did

  • Bug of the day: an empty "Untitled Note" appeared uninvited, and my controls couldn't remove it. Notes are getting a delete action and a hide for the panel.
  • The media window was standing around while the app reported it closed — removing the idle surface, and the media grid, titles and input targets now stay hidden until I explicitly ask to open, show or play something.
  • The screen-mirroring pairing question: "is there a way to always have it paired?" — automatic reconnection is on the list.
  • Shipped as a front-end-only update: idle media surface removed, first checks pass, no service restart or forced headset refresh.

Why / what I learned

  • Panels that appear without being asked are worse than missing features — they make the space feel haunted. "Only when requested" is the rule for every surface.
  • Small fixes still count as days: the goal is that every session leaves the room a little more predictable.

Next

  • Note deletion, panel visibility rules, screen-mirroring auto-pairing.

item.title: Day 6 — Ada drives Chrome from inside the headset
item.description: From VR, Ada switches Chrome tabs on the Mac, fills our YC draft and helps write the answers — while wireless ADB starts reconnecting itself and failures stop going silent.
item.content:encoded:
What I did

  • New rule in the design contract: every item should be relocatable by voice — not just Ada. The mirrored screen couldn't move to the second desk by name; that's now logged as an implementation gap, not a limitation.
  • Wireless ADB now reconnects itself on a new XR session: one bounded startup attempt with the saved headset address, identity verified before showing green, no cable and no screenshot. Confirmed live — "the ADB wireless started up connected right away."
  • Fixed the listening hang: after a quiet noise-only attempt, Ada returns to listening promptly instead of blocking my next sentence until a minute-long timeout.
  • Fixed the silence on failure: when a spatial action failed, the action-verification gate swallowed the entire final reply. Now the explanation still arrives — deployed and tested.
  • First real remote-control demo: from inside VR, Ada switched Chrome to the YC application tab, maximized it, typed our company name and a one-line description, saved, and verified after reload. "Yay! Cool, thanks. It worked."
  • Built a spatial working-note flow for the application: Ada asks follow-up questions, captures decisions, keeps brainstorming separate from approved wording, saves on request — and fills the form only after approval. Never submit.
  • Ada's first-pass answer, drafted from the build itself: "Gamology Space is building a context-aware interface for working with AI… AdaXR brings an AI collaborator into a mixed reality workspace."
  • Screenshot review caught the working note rendering as a one-line preview, full text intact but presentation broken. Being fixed as wrapped, scrollable text — and finished task cubes that never close are being chased too.

Why / what I learned

  • The assistant stops being a chat window when it can operate the same tools I use. Chrome on the Mac is the first demo — point at the work, talk about it, let Ada do the typing.
  • The YC form is a good forcing function: a real task with real stakes exposes everything the demo usually hides — notes that don't render, replies that don't arrive, cubes that won't close.

Next

  • Finish the note rendering and worker-cube lifecycle fixes, retest pointing-based movement, and keep pushing the remote-control flow.

item.title: Day 5 — Ada gets eyes
item.description: Screenshots from the headset land in a movable photo panel, the main window shows vision + ADB status at a glance, and screen mirroring starts becoming its own billboarded view.
item.content:encoded:
What I did

  • Gave Ada eyes: Quest screenshots now land in a movable photo panel inside the app. She read my equipment rack back from a fresh capture — Dell monitor, drive bays, green LEDs, cables. "It worked!"
  • Added a status window: vision permission and wireless ADB as separate red/green lines, checked every few seconds, with stale results expiring. Now I can see at a glance whether "go to the whiteboard" is actually possible.
  • Gave the photo panel real UI: detached from the vision menu, billboards toward my head, near-hand grab, two-hand resize (out = bigger, in = smaller), red close box — distance grab is next.
  • Started the screen-mirroring rework: the stream becomes a standalone billboarded view that stays where I put it, with its own stop control; the settings menu can move or close without killing it.
  • Movement bug batch: found why released ducklings snap into a line (a settling step returns them to fixed resting slots), why a drag cancels and snaps back (a change in the other hand cancels it), and caught combine breaking with the grid on — plus queue scrolling past three messages and palm targets still dropping.
  • Fixed failure communication: an action gate was suppressing the whole final reply when a move failed, honest explanation included. Now a blocked action still tells me why. 1,547 tests, staged for the headset.

Why / what I learned

  • "Can you see this?" becomes a real question once screenshots work. The status lights mean I don't have to guess whether the headset is connected before asking for something.
  • Most of the day was the unglamorous middle: capture mismatches, snapback paths, stale status. Failure paths deserve the same care as features — especially when the assistant is supposed to be trustworthy.

Next

  • Exact palm targeting, drag-release retention, finished-cube cleanup, combine with grid on, and the first live screen-stream test.

item.title: Day 4 — keep listening, and Ada learns to move
item.description: Hold an index finger up and pauses stop cutting my speech off; by evening Ada glides to the whiteboard on command with her ducklings trailing — and the daily log gets a repo that turns one note into posts for six platforms.
item.content:encoded:
What I did

  • Shipped "keep listening": hold either index finger up and a pause no longer ends the message mid-thought. Held my finger through a long pause — still listening. "A much needed feature so I don't get cut off."
  • Killed yesterday's magic-phrase bug for good: deletes now take natural wording, tied to the surface I selected — no synonym lists, no confirmation ritual.
  • Sub-agents learned to close when they're done, and the little worker cubes now follow Ada around like ducklings — my workshop crew, visible under the main cube.
  • Verified the audio fix: what Ada speaks now matches the chat exactly. "That part is working. And so good job."
  • Saved workspace revision 6 — five deletions and a server-rack rename persisted, floor intact. The build passed all 1,114 tests and the deployed version was verified live.
  • Relocation came alive: "move Ada to the whiteboard" → she glides there instead of teleporting; palm-reticle targeting landed ("It worked beautifully"); the ducklings trail her real path, bending around turns instead of sliding in a row.
  • Set the interaction rule: a named destination beats whatever my hand happens to be selecting — and in normal use the grid disappears entirely; you just say where she should go.
  • Set up this repo — every day's note now becomes the page you're reading plus copy-paste posts for X, Threads, Instagram, Facebook, TikTok and YouTube. No API keys, no autoposting; I post by hand.

Why / what I learned

  • "A pause shouldn't mean you've finished thinking" — the best line of the day, and the right bar for the interaction: hold my intent, don't make me hold its rules.
  • Ada's movement is basic right now, but it's headed somewhere deliberate: leave her on the desk, have her follow me around, or tell her a place and she hovers there. Position and animation are the visual cue that makes her feel present — the foundation for the embodiment work ahead.
  • The loop is becoming the product: issue in the headset → sub-agent builds the fix → release deploys → headset confirms it — all in one day.

Next

  • Movement cleanup: drag-release position, palm-target capture, finished worker cubes that stay open, and combine-with-grid-on — then more browser testing.

item.title: Day 3 — the room becomes editable
item.description: Seven test sessions, one loop: Ada can now name, relabel and delete the room around me — 8 surfaces deleted, 5 labels kept, all saved as workspace revision 5.
item.content:encoded:
What I did

  • Ran the whole day as one loop: test in the headset, log the issue, spawn sub-agents, test again. Seven sessions between 15:51 and 20:33.
  • Naming got solid — select a surface, tag it, rename it. Main desk, main screen, whiteboard, walls, server rack.
  • And then the big one: delete, for real. A request in the evening session, live before that session ended. Eight surfaces deleted and five renames kept by the end of the day.
  • The breakthrough moment: scene grid, blue outlines, name labels and the restored room all on at once. The room finally reads like an interface, not just a scan.
  • Learned the model that makes it safe: the app edits its own saved copy of the room scan — a snapshot. Move furniture for real and it won't follow, and the original Quest scan is never touched.
  • Fixed the speech mid-day: voice was cutting off, chat had junk "unspoken words," and replies landed as one giant text block. Now updates stream as they happen.
  • Ended by saving workspace revision 5: 50 surfaces, every renamed label retained, every deleted surface confirmed gone. The test suite went 801 → 915 along the way.

Why / what I learned

  • The room stops being a picture the moment you can edit it. Renaming a table is a small thing; realizing you can delete it and rebuild the space is the door opening.
  • The bug of the day came from the assistant being too literal — deletion demanded an exact phrase. "You shouldn't need a magic phrase." Intent, not incantations.

Next

  • File the queue of big fixes: the message queue needs to be visible and editable; sub-agents need to close themselves when they finish; and no more nine-minute stalls with zero feedback.

item.title: Day 2 — Ada grows hands
item.description: Every WebXR hand overlay on at once — joint markers, radius spheres, aim rays, orientation lines — plus a cyan index-finger ray and the first developer preset.
item.content:encoded:
What I did

  • Instrumented the hands, overlay by overlay, until every WebXR hand-tracking layer was live on both hands: white joint markers, wireframe radius spheres (each joint's reported size), orientation lines, and aiming rays.
  • Added a cyan ray out of the index finger, derived from the tracked finger joints. "Perfect. This is working perfectly." Hands prototyping for this stage: done.
  • Saved the combination as my first developer preset. It lives in project memory for now — "we have to do better than project memory, but we'll fix that later."
  • Identified the three mystery panels: the room panel, the capability catalog, and a browser-sharing panel that pipes a Mac Chrome tab into the headset — video, audio and input. That test comes next.
  • Asked for the dev-only menus to collapse into a single "developer settings" panel instead of cluttering the normal view.
  • Handed a speech bug to a sub-agent: Ada answered a sentence I never said. "I didn't say any of that. Let's book that as a bug."

Why / what I learned

  • Hands are how a room becomes an interface — if I can point at a surface and have Ada know exactly what I mean, the whole space becomes addressable.
  • Watching the raw tracking data while building against it is the whole trick: you can't debug an interaction you can't see.
  • Found a real one: long builds stop when the headset comes off. Not broken — just waiting — but work has to survive the headset leaving the head.

Next

  • Browser panel test: a Mac Chrome tab inside the headset — video and audio first, then clicking and scrolling.
  • Figure out why builds stall when the headset comes off.

item.title: Day 1 — Ada, take four
item.description: I'm officially starting the fourth attempt at Ada today — an assistant that lives in the room with me — and logging the whole attempt in the open, one day at a time.
item.content:encoded:
What I did

  • Started the fourth attempt at Ada today — officially. This is its first entry.
  • The frame for this attempt: Ada lives in the room. It's in the headset with me, in my actual scanned space — the grid, the outlines, every surface it can find and name. Voice in, voice out, and it runs its own little sub-agents while we work.
  • Set the rules for this log: one entry per build day, written that day, honest about what broke, with the real quotes from real test sessions instead of a cleaned-up story later.

Why / what I learned

  • Attempt four gets a trail. If this one works, the day-by-day of how it got there — including everything that didn't work — is the interesting part. It's the part nobody usually gets to see.
  • Open development from day one: these notes go up as they're written, not once they're pretty. The mistakes are part of the material.

Next

  • First build sessions in the headset. Bring the room up, and start with what Ada can find, see and name in it.
